verdict_evidence: ch2:136 '3.01 GB/seq at canonical context'; 24.1/8=3.01 is 9.2K input basis while :134 labels 9.5K/24.9 resident (3.11).

chapter_hint: Chapter 2 — What Actually Happens During Inference
page_hint: Ch 2 §6, Architecture Consequence, prefill levers bullet
quoted_clause: Changing format at the same byte width (BF16 in place of FP16) changes neither the bytes stored nor the H100 dense tensor-core peak: it trades mantissa bits (10 → 8) for exponent range
observed: The text says BF16 trades mantissa bits from 10 to 8 relative to FP16. BF16 has 7 explicit fraction bits (8 bits of significand precision including the implicit leading bit), while FP16 has 10 explicit fraction bits (11 bits of significand precision). The stated 10 → 8 is not the correct bit accounting.
correction: Replace “trades mantissa bits (10 → 8) for exponent range” with an accurate statement, e.g. “trades fraction bits (10 → 7) for exponent range” or “trades significand precision (11 → 8 bits including the implicit leading bit) for exponent range.”
acceptance_test: Verify the revised sentence against IEEE 754 binary16 and bfloat16 definitions; the stated bit counts must match the standard and must not imply BF16 has 8 explicit fraction bits.
verdict_evidence: chapter-02.md:164 'trades mantissa bits (10 -> 8)'; binary16 has 10 fraction bits, bfloat16 has 7; correct pair 10 -> 7 (or 11 -> 8 significand).
fix_instruction: Replace with 'trades fraction bits (10 -> 7) for exponent range' (or 'significand precision (11 -> 8 bits)').

chapter_hint: Chapter 2 — What Actually Happens During Inference
quoted_clause: or fewer input tokens (retrieval quality, prefix reuse)
observed: Prefix reuse is listed as a way to reduce input tokens. Prefix caching/KV reuse does not reduce the number of input tokens in the request; it avoids recomputing K/V for a shared prefix. It can reduce effective prefill compute, but the prompt still contains those tokens and they may still be billed depending on provider policy.
correction: Rewrite to separate the levers: “fewer input tokens (retrieval quality, context compression) or less prefill work for the same tokens (prefix reuse).”
acceptance_test: Confirm the revised sentence no longer claims prefix reuse reduces input-token count, and that it is consistent with the Ch 2 vocabulary table’s definition of prefix caching.
verdict_evidence: chapter-02.md:133 'fewer input tokens (retrieval quality, prefix reuse)'; vocabulary table (:35) defines prefix caching as work saving on same tokens, not token-count cut.
fix_instruction: 'fewer input tokens (retrieval quality, context compression) or less prefill work for the same tokens (prefix reuse)'.

page_hint: Chapter 2, §6 Architecture Consequence, prefill levers bullet
quoted_clause: Changing format at the same byte width (BF16 in place of FP16) changes neither the bytes stored nor the H100 dense tensor-core peak: it trades mantissa bits (10 → 8) for exponent range, a numerical-stability choice rather than a throughput one.
observed: FP16 has 10 explicit mantissa bits (11 including the implicit bit); BF16 has 7 explicit mantissa bits (8 including the implicit bit). The parenthetical 10 → 8 mixes explicit and total precision and is not correct as written.
correction: Change to 'it trades mantissa precision (10 explicit bits, or 11 including the implicit bit, for 7 explicit, or 8 including the implicit bit) for exponent range' or simply 'it trades precision for exponent range'.
acceptance_test: A reader can state FP16 and BF16 explicit mantissa widths correctly from the sentence.
verdict_evidence: ch2:164 'trades mantissa bits (10 -> 8)'; FP16 has 10 explicit (11 implicit), BF16 has 7 (8 implicit); pairing mixes conventions.
fix_instruction: Change to 'trades mantissa precision for exponent range', or '10 -> 7 explicit bits (11 -> 8 with implicit)'.

page_hint: Chapter 2, §2 Mental Model, decode bandwidth-bound paragraph
quoted_clause: It is like pushing the water of that same 140 GB reservoir through a standard garden hose: the whole volume must flow every 25 milliseconds just to deliver one glass of water — one generated token. The reservoir is not drained — the same 140 GB is re-read every step. The pump (compute) is more than powerful enough, but the diameter of the hose (HBM bandwidth) physically cannot move that volume of water in that time frame.
observed: This describes a single-device 140 GB weight stream requiring 5.6 TB/s, but the canonical host is 8×H100 with the weight sharded to 17.5 GB/GPU, requiring 700 GB/s per GPU and taking ~5.2 ms, which the later canonical host verdict says is inside the 25 ms TPOT budget and not HBM-saturating. The analogy's 'physically cannot move' is a capacity claim that conflicts with the canonical host feasibility.
correction: Reword to distinguish the batch-1-equivalent single-device illustration from the canonical 8×H100 host: e.g. 'In the single-device illustration, the 140 GB logical weight footprint would need 5.6 TB/s through one H100's hose; on the canonical 8×H100 host the same step is sharded to 17.5 GB/GPU (700 GB/s), so the step is memory-dominated but not HBM-saturating.'
acceptance_test: The analogy no longer implies the canonical 8×H100 host cannot meet the 25 ms TPOT due to HBM saturation, and it matches the later 17.5 GB/GPU arithmetic.
verdict_evidence: ch2:78 presents 140 GB every 25 ms through one hose as canonical; ch2:134 on 8xH100 shards to 17.5 GB/GPU = 5.2 ms 'inside budget'; ch2:136 'not HBM-saturating'.
fix_instruction: Add one clause: the 140 GB hose is the single-device illustration — on the 8xH100 host the step shards to 17.5 GB/GPU (5.2 ms), not saturating.

page_hint: Ch 2 §3 'Worked Example' — 'Occupancy thresholds' paragraph (after the 'Canonical host verdict' bullet)
quoted_clause: At the canonical operating point the 5.2 ms weight read is not HBM-saturating; it saturates HBM above ~5 concurrent sequences per GPU (~40 per host) only in the batch-1-equivalent case where each sequence streams its own full 17.5 GB shard, with no weight-read amortization.
observed: As written, the first clause is false for the canonical host. The 5.2 ms figure IS the time to stream the 17.5 GB shard at peak HBM bandwidth: 17.5 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 5.22 ms, i.e. 100% of peak. The sentence appears to intend 'the weight read does not saturate HBM for the whole 25 ms step', but the literal reading tells the reader that a single sequence leaves the memory system idle — the opposite of the truth, and the opposite of the decode-bandwidth-bound verdict the same chapter establishes.
correction: Rewrite as two explicit statements: (a) 'At batch 1 the 17.5 GB shard read takes 5.2 ms at peak HBM bandwidth — i.e. the weight read alone saturates HBM for 5.2 ms of the 25 ms step, so the step is bandwidth-bound, not idle.' (b) 'Under a no-amortization model in which each of B sequences independently streams the full shard, the aggregate demand reaches the 3.35 TB/s ceiling at B ~ 4.8 sequences per GPU (~40 per host) within the 25 ms budget; no production engine behaves this way (a real engine reads the shard once per step for the whole batch), so this is an upper bound, not an operating point.' Rename the second case (e.g. 'no-amortization upper bound') so it does not collide with 'batch-1-equivalent'.
acceptance_test: A reader who computes 17.5 GB / 3.35 TB/s from the text reaches 5.2 ms and finds the sentence consistent with their own arithmetic; the two batching models are named distinctly and each threshold is traceable to one of them.
verdict_evidence: ch02:136 'the 5.2 ms weight read is not HBM-saturating' false literally: 17.5 GB/5.2 ms = 3.37 TB/s = 100% of 3.35 peak; ~5-seq threshold is separate 25 ms-budget statement.
fix_instruction: Replace 'is not HBM-saturating' with 'moves 21% of peak over the 25 ms step (5.2 ms at peak)'; call the ~5-seq case 'no-amortization'.

quoted_clause: the attention portion reads KV cache at an intensity of only ~1–8 FLOP/byte and stays bandwidth-bound at every realistic batch size
observed: The '~1–8' range is unexplained. For the canonical full-MHA FP16 model the attention intensity is exactly 1 FLOP/byte; 8 FLOP/byte corresponds to an 8:1 GQA geometry (attention FLOPs are unchanged by head sharing while KV bytes fall by the sharing factor). The reader cannot tell which end applies to the canonical model, and the range reads as measurement scatter rather than as an architectural dependence.
correction: Write it as: 'the attention portion reads KV cache at ~1 FLOP/byte for the canonical full-MHA FP16 geometry (and ~8 FLOP/byte for an 8:1 GQA geometry, since head sharing cuts KV bytes without cutting attention FLOPs) — in either case far below the ~295 ridge, so it stays bandwidth-bound at every realistic batch size.'
acceptance_test: Each end of the quoted intensity range is tied to a named geometry, and the canonical model's value is stated unambiguously.
verdict_evidence: ch2:136 '~1-8 FLOP/byte' in canonical-host paragraph where model is full-MHA (ch3:196); AI=1 for MHA, 8 only for 8:1 GQA; neither end tied to geometry.
fix_instruction: Ch2:136 — replace '~1–8 FLOP/byte' with '~1 FLOP/byte for the full-MHA canonical model (~8 for an 8:1 GQA geometry)'.
